pages.title: A mixed redox problem needs a bookkeeping plan

blocks.text: A reaction may be presented as a salt formula, an unbalanced ionic equation or a cell diagram. Before choosing a method, identify what is being asked: oxidation state, agent, balance, stoichiometric amount or electron-flow direction.
In the following teacher-created practice cases, first assign states, then identify the changes. Atom and charge checks connect the symbolic chemistry to a physically possible transfer.

pages.transition: Begin by using charge balance to find an unknown state.

pages.title: Case one: oxidation numbers with an exception

blocks.text: For MnO₄⁻, let Mn be x and O be −2. x − 8 = −1, giving x = +7. For CaO₂, Ca is +2 and the two O must total −2, so O is −1. The peroxide exception prevents the incorrect assignment Ca = +4.
Rules must be applied in a sensible order. Recognise a peroxide or hydride before using the usual oxygen or hydrogen assignment blindly.
The algebraic oxidation-number sum equals the whole species charge: zero for a neutral compound, the ion charge for a polyatomic ion.

pages.transition: Now use the assignments to identify disproportionation.

pages.title: Case two: one state splits into two

blocks.text: Balance the disproportionation skeleton Mn³⁺ → Mn²⁺ + MnO₂ in acid. One Mn changes +3 → +2, gaining one electron; another changes +3 → +4, losing one. Start with 2Mn³⁺. Balance O and H to obtain 2Mn³⁺ + 2H₂O → Mn²⁺ + MnO₂ + 4H⁺. Charge is +6 on each side.
Mn³⁺ acts as both oxidant and reductant. The product distribution balances the total increase and decrease; simply writing one Mn³⁺ on the left would lose a manganese atom.

pages.transition: For a different redox pair, split the process into explicit halves.

pages.title: Case three: balance an acidic ionic reaction

blocks.text: Teacher-created example: balance MnO₄⁻ oxidising Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ in acid, with Mn²⁺ product. Reduction is MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O. Oxidation is Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻. Multiply oxidation by five, add, and cancel: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O + 5Fe³⁺.
Left charge is −1 + 8 + 10 = +17; right is +2 + 15 = +17. The permanganate accepts five electrons per Mn, fixing the 1:5 mole ratio.

pages.transition: The basic-medium form must remove introduced protons.

pages.title: Case four: balance a basic disproportionation

blocks.text: For Cl₂ → Cl⁻ + ClO⁻ in base, one Cl goes 0 → −1 and one 0 → +1. Balance first in acid: Cl₂ + H₂O → Cl⁻ + ClO⁻ + 2H⁺. Add 2OH⁻ to both sides and combine H⁺ + OH⁻ into water. Cancel one H₂O, giving Cl₂ + 2OH⁻ → Cl⁻ + ClO⁻ + H₂O.
A final basic equation should not retain unexplained H⁺. Adding OH⁻ to only one side would violate charge conservation; neutralisation is performed on both sides.

pages.transition: Use the balanced coefficients to convert a measured amount.

pages.title: Case five: stoichiometry from electron conservation

blocks.text: Teacher-created titration calculation: 0.00150 mol Cr₂O₇²⁻ reacts completely with Fe²⁺ in acid. The balanced ratio is 1 dichromate : 6 Fe²⁺, so n(Fe²⁺) = 6 × 0.00150 = 0.00900 mol. If this was in 50.0 mL, c = 0.00900/0.0500 = 0.180 mol L⁻¹.
A charge of −2 on dichromate is not its electron-transfer number. Each of its two Cr(+6) becomes Cr(+3), giving six accepted electrons in total.

pages.transition: Separate the half-reactions to describe a galvanic cell.

pages.title: Case six: a zinc–silver cell

blocks.text: Anode: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻. Cathode: 2Ag⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2Ag. Net: Zn + 2Ag⁺ → Zn²⁺ + 2Ag. Zinc is oxidised, Ag⁺ reduced, and electrons flow externally from Zn toward the silver electrode.

In a galvanic cell the anode is negative and cathode positive. Ions move through the electrolyte and bridge to prevent charge accumulation. Electrode mass can change: zinc loses mass while silver deposits at the cathode.

pages.transition: An externally driven process can use different electrode chemistry.

pages.title: Case seven: electrode material can matter

blocks.text: Electrolysis uses external electrical energy to drive an electrode process. Oxidation still occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode, but one must examine the electrolyte and whether the electrode itself can react.

In AgNO₃ solution, a silver anode can dissolve as Ag → Ag⁺ + e⁻. A platinum anode does not supply silver this way; another solution process must carry oxidation. This introductory comparison explains why an electrode is not always an inert label. Detailed selection of products requires further electrochemical information.

pages.transition: Return to a chemical application and check oxygen, charge and agent roles.

pages.title: Case eight: remove chlorine through a redox reaction

blocks.text: Teacher-created balance: Cl₂ + SO₂ + 2H₂O → 2Cl⁻ + SO₄²⁻ + 4H⁺. Sulfur changes +4 → +6 and loses two electrons. Two chlorine atoms each gain one electron, changing 0 → −1. Charge right is −2 −2 +4 = 0, matching the neutral left; all atoms also match.
Chlorine is the oxidising agent and sulfur dioxide the reducing agent. The equation demonstrates that oxidation does not require adding an O₂ molecule directly to the reductant.
A balanced equation establishes conservation, but experimental usefulness still depends on conditions and feasibility. Balance alone does not guarantee a reaction proceeds rapidly.

pages.transition: Revise a complete method-selection route before attempting the final questions.

pages.title: Revision: state, change, balance and interpret

blocks.text: Assign oxidation states with exceptions; distinguish real charge from formal averages. Identify oxidation increases, reduction decreases and the corresponding reductant/oxidant. For disproportionation, one element supplies both changes.

Balance half-reactions for the given medium, cancel electrons, and verify atoms plus total charge. Convert quantities using the balanced mole ratio. In cells, oxidation is at the anode, reduction at the cathode; electrons use the external circuit and ions the internal path.

questions.question: Is CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ redox?
questions.answer: No. Oxidation states do not change even though decomposition occurs.

questions.question: In 2Mn³⁺ + 2H₂O → Mn²⁺ + MnO₂ + 4H⁺, which species has both agent roles?
questions.answer: Mn³⁺, because it is reduced to +2 and oxidised to +4.

questions.question: How many Fe²⁺ react with 0.00200 mol MnO₄⁻ in the stated acidic reaction?
questions.answer: The ratio is 5:1, so 0.0100 mol Fe²⁺.

questions.question: Why is dichromate’s −2 charge not its electron-transfer number?
questions.answer: Its two Cr atoms each gain three electrons on forming Cr³⁺, so the total is six.

questions.question: What is the electron-flow direction in a zinc–silver galvanic cell?
questions.answer: From zinc anode through the external wire to the silver cathode, where Ag⁺ is reduced.

questions.question: Does an electrolytic anode always remain chemically unchanged?
questions.answer: No. An active electrode can be oxidised itself, such as a silver anode supplying Ag⁺.

questions.question: Why is checking atoms alone insufficient?
questions.answer: An ionic equation must also conserve total charge, and its coupled halves must transfer equal electron counts.
